p: Al-Malik az-Zahir Ghiyath ud-din Ghazi was the third son of Saladin. In 1186, when he was 15, his father appointed him governor of Aleppo, Mosul and the neighbouring areas recently taken from the Zengids, lands that had been under the control of Saladin's brother al-Adil. His two older brothers received Syria (al-Afdal) and Egypt (al-Aziz) at the same time. When he inherited in 1193 he was to owe suzerainty to al-Afdal in Damascus, but he conducted his affairs independently and for a while stayed out of his brothers' quarrels with their uncle.

In 1193 he called on al-Adil for troops to put down the revolt of the Zengid Izz al-Din in Mosul. The next year he received Latakia and Jableh in a settlement by which he recognised al-Afdal's authority, but in 1196 he joined al-Aziz and al-Adil in deposing and exiling that brother. In October 1197, with Bohemond III of Antioch threatening Latakia and Jableh, he destroyed the two ports; Bohemond took them, found them of no use and withdrew, and az-Zahir reoccupied them and rebuilt the fortress at Latakia. He kept many of his father's advisers and appointed Baha ad-Din as a judge in Aleppo.

After al-Aziz died in 1198, az-Zahir allied with al-Afdal, and with most of the other Ayyubid princes they besieged Damascus. The city held out for months, and he withdrew his troops. Al-Adil, having conquered Egypt, returned, reduced az-Zahir's territories to the area around Aleppo and forced him to recognise his suzerainty. In his last decade az-Zahir skirmished with crusaders and lent his army to other Ayyubid princes. King Leo of Cilicia defeated his forces at the Battle of Amq in 1206 but gained no lasting advantage against Aleppo, and in 1207 his troops lifted a siege of Homs.

In 1212 az-Zahir married Dayfa Khatun, the daughter of his old rival al-Adil, a match that ended the rivalry between the two branches of the family. Before his death he appointed his younger son al-Aziz Muhammad, born in 1213, to succeed him. He died on 8 October 1216. His lands had included northern Syria and a small part of Mesopotamia.

notes: The article says he brought the 'unorthodox as-Suhrawardi' to Aleppo and was forced to imprison him in 1191 on the demand of the orthodox ulama; it does not say what became of him, so I left the episode out.
The article says 'the French attacked and besieged Homs' in 1207; I wrote only 'a siege of Homs'.
The article calls him 'the Kurdish Ayyubid emir'; not added.
The description says he kept Aleppo independent of al-Adil; the article says al-Adil forced him to recognise his suzerainty after the siege of Damascus. The editor may want to adjust the description.
